qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between GDP per capita and an individual’s actual income.
items.canonical_answer: GDP per capita is output divided by population, an average. An individual’s income depends on the actual distribution and sources of receipts, so it need not equal the average.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): output/population average. Contrast/test (1): individual distribution can differ.
objective_titles: Describe simple measures and indicators of comparative living standards

items.prompt: Calculate real GDP per capita from invented real GDP N$120 million and population 10,000.
items.canonical_answer: Real GDP per capita = real GDP / population = N$120,000,000 / 10,000 = N$12,000 per person.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): N$120m/10,000. Result/units (1): N$12,000 per person.
objective_titles: Describe simple measures and indicators of comparative living standards

items.prompt: Analyse a living-standard comparison with equal real GDP per person in two invented districts, but A has concentrated income and limited water access while B has broad income distribution and reliable water access.
items.canonical_answer: The average output measure is equal but access and distribution differ. B has stronger evidence of broadly shared material conditions; equality of GDP per person does not prove equal living standards or every individual’s position.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): equal averages, different conditions. Evidence (1): distribution/water contrast. Explanation (2): averages conceal access (1), individual and other indicators remain relevant (1).
objective_titles: Describe simple measures and indicators of comparative living standards

items.prompt: Explain the error in claiming disposable income is already real income because direct taxes have been subtracted.
items.canonical_answer: Disposable income adjusts for tax and relevant transfers; real income adjusts for prices. Subtracting tax alone does not establish purchasing power.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): tax adjustment equated with price adjustment. Boundary/test (1): prices needed for real measure.
objective_titles: Describe simple measures and indicators of comparative living standards

items.prompt: Explain why a 10% total real-income increase does not establish higher real income per capita if population rises 20%.
items.canonical_answer: Population grows faster than real income, so the amount per person falls. Aggregate and per-capita real measures have different denominators.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): total increase treated as per-person increase. Boundary/test (1): population grows faster, reducing ratio.
objective_titles: Describe simple measures and indicators of comparative living standards

items.prompt: Explain how unequal access to training and transport can contribute to income disparities where genuine jobs require the skill and reliable travel.
items.canonical_answer: Those with access can gain relevant skills and reach vacancies. Those without access face barriers even where they want work, leading to unequal earnings opportunities under the stated job conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): unequal access. Mechanism (2): skill eligibility (1), reachable jobs (1). Consequence (1): unequal earnings opportunities.
objective_titles: Describe differences in living standards and discuss reasons for disparities within nations and between nations, both developed and developing countries

items.prompt: Explain why a high-average-income country can still contain households with poor living conditions when income and services are unevenly distributed.
items.canonical_answer: The average can be raised by high-income groups while others lack resources or services. The country label does not establish each household’s access.
marking_guidance: Context (1): unequal distribution/services. Reason/conclusion (1): average masks household differences.
objective_titles: Describe differences in living standards and discuss reasons for disparities within nations and between nations, both developed and developing countries

items.prompt: Explain a living-standard benefit from a village learning hub with affordable devices, reliable connectivity, relevant materials and assistance.
items.canonical_answer: Usable access lets learners obtain resources without the previous long journey. Time and access barriers fall, improving learning opportunity under the stated affordability, reliability and skill conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): usable hub access. Mechanism (2): materials reachable (1), travel barrier reduced (1). Consequence (1): better opportunity conditional on effective use.
objective_titles: Explain the effect of Information Technology on living standards

items.prompt: Explain why putting a service online can widen disparities if only already advantaged households have affordable connectivity and digital skills.
items.canonical_answer: Connected households gain convenient access while excluded households cannot use the new route. Without alternative access or support, the benefits are uneven and the gap can widen.
marking_guidance: Context (1): unequal usable access. Reason/consequence (1): gains concentrated while others excluded.
objective_titles: Explain the effect of Information Technology on living standards

items.prompt: Define GDP per capita (2). Identify two non-income living-standard indicators (2). Explain a benefit of affordable usable online learning materials replacing a long journey (2). Identify two distributional differences in this invented comparison: A income concentrated and water access limited; B income broadly shared and water access reliable (2).
items.canonical_answer: GDP per capita is GDP divided by population, an average output measure. Education and safe-water access are indicators. Useful online materials can reduce travel and improve learning access when usable. B has broader income distribution and better water access than A.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): GDP/population (1), average output rather than actual individual income (1). Separate points for indicators (2): education (1), safe water (1). Explanation (2): travel barrier reduced (1), useful learning access (1). Identification (2): distribution contrast (1), water contrast (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented districts each have real GDP N$120m and population 10,000. A has concentrated income and limited water/school access; B has broadly shared income and reliable water/school access. Both receive online learning materials, but only B currently has affordable devices, reliable power/connectivity and assistance. Prices and definitions are consistent; no individual cash income is specified. Describe three comparison features with case details (6). Explain the per-capita calculation and the conditions for IT to improve useful household access (7). Discuss whether the equal averages establish equal living standards (7).
items.canonical_answer: Both have real GDP per capita N$12,000, but income distribution and service access differ. Dividing N$120m by 10,000 gives the average, not individual income. B’s devices, reliable connection and assistance allow materials to be used, reducing travel barriers. A’s excluded households may not gain. Equality of averages is insufficient; broader services and distribution favour B on the supplied dimensions, though other welfare evidence and individual variation remain relevant.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): equal real average (1), N$12,000 detail (1); income pattern (1), concentrated/broad detail (1); service difference (1), water/school detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): divide real GDP/population (1), N$12,000 result (1), not actual individual income (1); devices affordable (1), reliable power/connectivity (1), assistance/skills (1), useful materials reduce access barrier (1). Both sides/judgement (7): equal output average supplies one similarity (1), may indicate potential resources (1); distribution differs (1), service/IT access differs (1); condition other welfare facts and individual variation (1); judgement equality not established (1), B stronger broad-access evidence (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

facts: Invented districts each have real GDP N$120m and population 10,000. A has concentrated income and limited water/school access; B has broadly shared income and reliable water/school access. Both receive online learning materials, but only B currently has affordable devices, reliable power/connectivity and assistance. Prices and definitions are consistent; no individual cash income is specified.

items.prompt: Invented economies with the same real GDP per person. Case 1: income highly concentrated, remote households lack reliable water and schooling, IT access favours already affluent groups. Case 2: income more broadly shared and reliable water, schooling and usable IT are widely accessible. No pollution, leisure or individual-health data are supplied. Evaluate the claim that the average demonstrates high living standards throughout Case 1 (7). Evaluate the strength and limits of the broad living-standard case in Case 2 (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: the real average is useful about output resources, but concentration and service gaps prevent an all-household inference; IT access can reinforce the divide. Case 2: broad income and services support a stronger shared material-access case, but averages and access figures do not reveal all individual outcomes, environmental costs or leisure. The supplied dimensions favour Case 2 while a complete welfare comparison remains conditional.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for output-average relevance (1), potential resources (1); argument against concentration (1), service/IT exclusion (1); condition household and other welfare evidence needed (1); judgement throughout claim unsupported (1), tied to distribution/access (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for broad resources (1), services/IT access (1); argument against individual variation (1), missing environmental/leisure evidence (1); condition dimensions and coverage stated (1); judgement stronger shared material case (1), not complete welfare proof (1). Total 14.

Case 2: income more broadly shared and reliable water, schooling and usable IT are widely accessible. No pollution, leisure or individual-health data are supplied.
